title: How long a habit takes
hook: a 2009 study found new habits took 18 to 254 days, a median of 66 (Lally et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the talking mind. Did you catch the voice mid-sentence and name it: planning, replaying, judging? Which one showed up most? Day three hundred ten.

You've probably heard it. It takes twenty-one days to form a habit. It's on posters, in apps, in pep talks. It sounds precise and it sounds doable: three weeks and you're a new person. So people start in January, push hard for three weeks, and on day twenty-two they wait for the habit to carry them. It doesn't. And they decide something is wrong with them. Here's the good news. Nothing is wrong with them. The number was wrong. In 2009, a team in London actually measured it. Today: how long a habit takes.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE DAYS, THEY SAY.` → `DAY TWENTY-TWO: NOTHING.` → `THE NUMBER WAS WRONG.`

segments.voice: Start with where twenty-one came from. In 1960 a plastic surgeon named Maxwell Maltz wrote a bestselling book in which he observed that patients took a minimum of about twenty-one days to get used to a change, like a new face in the mirror. A minimum, for getting used to something. Over the years it became a rule for building anything. Now the measurement. Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London asked about ninety volunteers to pick one new daily behavior, like a glass of water with breakfast or a walk before dinner, done in the same situation each day. Every day they rated how automatic it felt. Then the team watched the curve. It rose quickly at first, then flattened out as the behavior became automatic. The middle of the pack got there in about sixty-six days. But the range was huge: some people took eighteen days, and for some the curve was so slow the team estimated about two hundred fifty. Harder behaviors took longer. And one finding is worth keeping close. Missing a single day didn't meaningfully set people back. The habit didn't reset to zero. William James said it in 1890, in his chapter on habit: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Ally takes time. And long before him, Aristotle noticed that in Greek the words for character and for habit are nearly the same word, ethos, and he argued that we become just by doing just things, over and over. So sixty-six is not a deadline. It's a middle. If you're on day forty and it still feels like effort, you're not failing. You're in the middle.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE WAS A MINIMUM, FOR ADJUSTING.` · `A MEDIAN OF 66 DAYS.` · `18 TO 254: A HUGE RANGE.` · `MISSING ONE DAY DIDN'T RESET IT.` · then, large: `66 DAYS, ROUGHLY.`

segments.voice: Use the two minutes to choose. Think of one practice from this path you'd like to keep, maybe the six slow breaths, or naming the talking mind. Now tie it to one moment you already have every day: waking, the first coffee, sitting in the car before you turn the key. Say it to yourself as one sentence. When this happens, I do that. Then just sit with the choice. The bell holds the time.
How long a habit takes. In one careful study, a median of about sixty-six days, anywhere from eighteen to around two hundred fifty. Today's word.
screen: `HOW LONG A HABIT TAKES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: 66 days, roughly. Do today's practice after your chosen moment, and if you miss one day this week, remember: it doesn't reset. Day three hundred ten.

howItsDone: Habit researchers track how automatic a repeated behavior feels over weeks; people building a practice often do it daily in the same situation and expect it to take a couple of months, not three weeks.

fork.setup: day forty of a new practice. it still takes effort every morning. what does the study suggest?
options: you've failed: it should be automatic by now.
you're in the middle: keep going.
fork.reveal: the median was about 66 days and some took far longer. effort on day forty is normal.

original.note: Greek: habit, custom; Aristotle tied ēthos, character, to it.

trapdoor: what you thought: three weeks and it sticks.
what it means: about two months in the middle of the pack, with a huge range.
what a scholar hears: Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology, measuring automaticity curves that rise and then plateau.

notes: Lally et al.: 96 volunteers, 12 weeks, eating/drinking/activity behaviors in a consistent context; median 66 days to 95% of plateau, range 18–254 (the upper figures extrapolated). Confirm 'about ninety'.
Maltz (1960) wording: 'a minimum of about 21 days'; confirm the paraphrase.
James quotation (Principles, ch. IV 'Habit'): confirm exact wording.

Aristotle, NE II.1: ēthikē (moral virtue) from ethos (habit), 'hence its name'; the script simplifies to 'the word for character sits next to the word for habit'. The Greek words are ἦθος (character, eta) and ἔθος (habit, epsilon); a reviewer may want the distinction spelled out. The line 'we become what we repeatedly do' is a paraphrase of NE II.1, not a quotation (the popular 'we are what we repeatedly do' is Will Durant's summary).
